title: The eight parts of speech
blurb: Name the part of speech of any word by the job it does in the sentence, including words that switch jobs.
question: In “After the shift ended, Rosa drove home” and “Rosa drove home after her shift,” the word “after” has two different jobs. What part of speech is it in each sentence, and how can you tell in under a minute?

teach.h: Words are named by their job
teach.body: Formally, a part of speech is the grammatical class a word belongs to, decided by the role it plays in its sentence. English has eight: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. Plain English: you cannot tell a word's part of speech from its spelling alone. “Report” is a noun in “the report” and a verb in “report any pain.” Find what the word is doing in THIS sentence, then name it.

teach.caption: Articles (a, an, the) and pointing words before a noun (that chart, my chart) act as adjectives.
In “has been resting,” has and been are helpers and resting is the main verb. Feel, look, taste and smell can be action or linking verbs.

teach.h: Before, after, since, until: which job?
teach.caption: The same test sorts “that”: before a noun (that chart) it acts as an adjective; standing alone (That is mine) it is a pronoun.

teach.h: Sentence parts the HESI A2 names

rows.label: The aide handed the patient a cup.
The aide handed the patient a cup.
The chart is on the desk.

teach.note: Direct object = what receives the action. Indirect object = to or for whom. Subject complement follows a linking verb. Appositive = a noun that renames a noun.

teach.body: Nursing applicant Aaliyah James checks two practice sentences. In “After the shift ended, Rosa drove home,” a subject (the shift) and a verb (ended) follow “after,” so it is a subordinating conjunction. In “Rosa drove home after her shift,” only the noun phrase “her shift” follows, so “after” is a preposition and “shift” is its object. She spends five seconds on each: look right, find the verb or the noun, name the job.

teach.text: HESI A2 traps: calling an -ly adjective an adverb (friendly, lonely, costly describe nouns), calling “well” an adjective in “works well,” calling every “after,” “before” or “since” a conjunction (with only a noun after it, it is a preposition), and labeling a gerund (Walking helps) as a verb.

items: Judge each word by its job in this sentence, not by its spelling.
Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs (very calm, works slowly).
Linking verbs (seem, become, feel, look) connect the subject to a description.
Before, after, since, until: subject + verb after it = conjunction; noun only = preposition.
Pronouns stand alone (hers, that, everyone); the same word before a noun acts as an adjective (that chart).
Know the sentence parts: direct object, indirect object, subject complement, appositive.

summary: You can now name all eight parts of speech by the job each word does, including words such as after, that, fast and well that change jobs. You can also pick out helping and linking verbs and name the main sentence parts.

A.q: In the sentence “She seemed very calm after the long procedure,” what part of speech is the word “very”?
A.why: “Very” modifies the adjective “calm,” and words that modify adjectives are adverbs.

whyNot.0: Adjectives modify nouns; “very” modifies another describing word, calm.
whyNot.1: A preposition links a noun object to the sentence; “very” has no object.
whyNot.3: A pronoun replaces a noun; “very” replaces nothing.

A.q: In the sentence “The lonely patient waited quietly by the window,” which word is an adverb?
A.why: “Quietly” tells how the patient waited, so it modifies the verb “waited” and is an adverb.

whyNot.0: “Lonely” ends in -ly but describes the noun “patient,” so it is an adjective.
whyNot.2: “Window” names a thing, so it is a noun (the object of “by”).
whyNot.3: “By” takes the object “window,” so it is a preposition.

A.q: In the sentence “Swimming is good exercise for patients with arthritis,” what part of speech is the word “Swimming”?
A.why: “Swimming” is the subject of “is,” so this -ing form names an activity and acts as a noun (a gerund).

whyNot.0: An -ing adjective describes a noun (“a swimming pool”); here “Swimming” is the subject itself.
whyNot.1: The verb of the sentence is “is”; an -ing form with no helping verb is not the main verb.
whyNot.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; “Swimming” names the activity.

B.q: In the sentence “Ouch, the tape pulled at my skin,” what part of speech is the word “Ouch”?
B.why: “Ouch” expresses a sudden feeling and stands apart from the rest of the sentence, so it is an interjection.

whyNot.0: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; “Ouch” modifies nothing.
whyNot.2: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; “Ouch” names nothing.
whyNot.3: A conjunction joins words or clauses; “Ouch” joins nothing.

B.q: In the sentence “Those are the forms the surgeon signed,” what part of speech is the word “Those”?
B.why: “Those” stands alone as the subject of “are,” so it is a demonstrative pronoun.

whyNot.0: “Those” acts as an adjective only when a noun follows it (“those forms”); here it stands alone.
whyNot.1: A conjunction joins clauses; “Those” is the subject of the sentence.
whyNot.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; “Those” stands for the forms.

B.q: In the sentence “The nurse gave Mr. Diaz his discharge papers,” what is the function of “Mr. Diaz”?
B.why: “Mr. Diaz” tells to whom the papers were given, so he is the indirect object; “his discharge papers” is the direct object.

whyNot.0: The direct object is what was given: “his discharge papers.”
whyNot.2: A subject complement follows a linking verb; “gave” is an action verb.
whyNot.3: An appositive renames a noun beside it; “Mr. Diaz” does not rename “nurse.”

C.q: In which sentence is “since” a subordinating conjunction?
options: Since the clinic moved, parking has been easier.
Since Monday, parking has been much easier.
Parking has been easier since last spring.
Since the move in early May, parking is easier.
C.why: Here “since” is followed by a subject (the clinic) and a verb (moved), so it introduces a clause and is a subordinating conjunction.

whyNot.1: “Since Monday” has no verb, so “since” is a preposition.
whyNot.2: “Since last spring” has no verb, so “since” is a preposition.
whyNot.3: “The move” is a noun, not a subject-verb pair, so “since” is a preposition.

C.q: In the sentence “The patient has been feeling dizzy since breakfast,” what kind of verb is “has”?
C.why: “Has” helps form the verb phrase “has been feeling”; the main verb is “feeling,” so “has” is a helping (auxiliary) verb.

whyNot.0: “Feeling” is the verb that links the patient to “dizzy”; “has” only helps it.
whyNot.1: “Has” does not show an action here; it builds the tense.
whyNot.2: The main verb is the last verb in the phrase: “feeling.”

C.q: Which word in the sentence is a coordinating conjunction? “Although the patient was tired, she walked to the window, for she wanted fresh air.”
C.why: “For” (meaning because) joins two independent clauses after a comma, so it is a coordinating conjunction from FANBOYS.

whyNot.0: “Although” is a subordinating conjunction: it makes its clause dependent.
whyNot.1: “To” takes the object “window,” so it is a preposition here.
whyNot.2: “She” is a pronoun, the subject of “walked.”

reteach.title: Words are workers with job titles
reteach.question: Think of a sentence as a small team. Each word has a job today, and the same person can do a different job tomorrow. How do you tell who is doing what?

blocks.body: You cannot tell a worker's job from their name, only from what they are doing on this shift. “After” working in front of a full clause (after the shift ended) is a conjunction; working in front of a single noun (after her shift) it is a preposition; working alone (soon after) it is an adverb. “That” in front of a noun is describing it; “that” standing alone is filling in for it. Watch the job, then name the title.

steps.label: What does it touch?
steps.sub: a noun, a verb, a clause?

blocks.text: Spelling clues mislead: -ly does not guarantee an adverb (friendly, costly), and -ing does not guarantee a verb (Walking helps; a walking boot).

explain.body: An action verb shows something done. A linking verb (is, seem, become, feel) connects the subject to a word that describes or renames it. A helping verb (has, been, will, can) supports the main verb.

test.q: In the sentence “The patient felt dizzy after standing,” what kind of verb is “felt”?
test.why: “Felt” connects the subject (patient) to a describing word (dizzy), so it is a linking verb.

whyNot.0: The patient is not doing something to an object; “felt” links to a description.
whyNot.1: A helping verb supports another verb; here “felt” is the only verb.
whyNot.3: An infinitive is “to” plus a verb (to feel).

explain.body: Adjectives describe nouns and pronouns (what kind, which one, how many). Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs (how, when, where, how often, to what degree). An -ly ending is a clue, not a rule.

test.q: In the sentence “The costly repair was finished surprisingly fast,” what part of speech is the word “costly”?
test.why: “Costly” describes the noun “repair,” so it is an adjective even though it ends in -ly.

whyNot.0: An adverb would modify a verb, adjective or adverb; “costly” describes a noun.
whyNot.2: “Repair” is the noun; “costly” tells what kind of repair.
whyNot.3: The verb is “was finished”; “costly” shows no action.

explain.body: Words such as after, before, since and until can be either. Look right: a subject and verb mean a subordinating conjunction; a noun or pronoun alone means a preposition with an object.

test.q: In the sentence “Keep the dressing dry until the doctor removes it,” what part of speech is the word “until”?
test.why: A subject (the doctor) and a verb (removes) follow “until,” so it introduces a clause and is a subordinating conjunction.

whyNot.0: “Until” is a preposition only with a noun object alone (“until noon”).
whyNot.1: An adverb would stand without a clause after it.
whyNot.3: An adjective describes a noun; “until” joins a time clause to the main clause.

explain.body: This, that, these and those are pronouns when they stand alone and act as adjectives when a noun follows. Possessive forms work the same way: “hers” stands alone (pronoun); “her” before a noun acts as an adjective.

test.q: In the sentence “These belong in the sharps container,” what part of speech is the word “These”?
test.why: “These” stands alone as the subject of “belong,” so it is a demonstrative pronoun.

whyNot.0: “These” would act as an adjective with a noun after it (“These needles”).
whyNot.2: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb; “These” is the subject.
whyNot.3: A conjunction joins clauses; “These” begins the only clause.
